questions.stem: A client with depression says, "Things would be better if I weren't around." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?"
"You have so much to live for."
"Let's talk about this tomorrow."
"Everyone feels that way sometimes."

rationale.correct: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plan, means and intent.

perOption.a: Asking directly about suicide doesn't increase risk and is essential for assessment.
perOption.b: This dismisses the feeling and skips assessment.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: When is a client with severe depression at increased risk for suicide?

options.text: When antidepressant treatment starts to improve energy, about 10 to 14 days in
During the most severe, withdrawn phase only
Only after discharge
Never once medication is started

rationale.correct: Monitor closely as energy improves and in the early weeks of treatment, especially in young people.

perOption.a: More energy before mood lifts may give the client the energy to act on a plan.
perOption.b: Risk also rises as energy returns.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize periods of increased suicide risk.

questions.stem: A client at high risk for suicide is admitted. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Remove belts, shoelaces and other items that could be used for self-harm
Place the client on continuous one-to-one observation
Check the client's belongings and the room for hazards
Make a no-suicide contract instead of observation
Assign a room far from the nurses' station
Ask directly about thoughts of suicide regularly

rationale.correct: Suicide precautions: remove means, close observation, frequent assessment.

perOption.a: This removes the means.
perOption.e: The client should be near staff.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client who has been very depressed suddenly seems calm and cheerful and is giving away prized possessions. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: The client may have decided on a suicide plan
The depression has resolved
The medication is working perfectly
The client is ready for discharge

rationale.correct: Warning signs: sudden calm, giving things away, saying goodbye, putting affairs in order.

perOption.a: Sudden calm and giving away belongings are warning signs.
perOption.b: Sudden improvement can be a warning sign.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: The nurse reviews notes on a client with depression. Highlight the statements or behaviors that are suicide warning signs.

segments.text: "I won't be a burden to anyone much longer."
gave the dog to a neighbor
several saved-up pills in a sock
"I'm looking forward to my daughter's visit next week."

rationale.correct: Identify verbal, behavioral and situational warning signs of suicide.

perOption.s2: Talking about being a burden is a warning sign.
perOption.s4: Giving away possessions is a warning sign.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize suicide warning signs in documentation.

questions.stem: A client with severe depression isn't eating, isn't bathing and hasn't said anything about self-harm. Which need comes first after safety is confirmed?

options.text: Nutrition and fluid intake
Hygiene
Group therapy participation
Discharge planning

rationale.correct: Depression: safety first, then physiological needs (nutrition, sleep), then self-care and therapy.

perOption.a: Physiological needs come next after safety.
perOption.b: This matters but ranks after nutrition.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "You may be confused and have some memory loss for a while afterward."
"You'll be awake and feel the seizure."
"You can eat breakfast right before."
"One treatment cures depression permanently."

rationale.correct: ECT: informed consent, NPO, anesthesia and muscle relaxant; monitor for confusion and memory changes.

perOption.a: Short-term confusion and memory loss are common and usually temporary.
perOption.b: General anesthesia and a muscle relaxant are used.
perOption.d: A series of treatments is usual.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client in acute mania won't sit down to eat and has lost weight. What should the nurse offer?

options.text: High-calorie finger foods the client can eat while moving
A large meal at a table with others
Three small meals only
Nothing until the client sits down

rationale.correct: Mania: finger foods, fluids, reduced stimulation and rest periods.

perOption.a: Portable foods meet energy needs.
perOption.b: The client can't sit, and it's overstimulating.
perOption.c: This isn't enough for high energy needs.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with mania is loud, intrusive and interrupting other clients' activities. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Set clear, consistent limits and guide the client to a quieter area
Encourage the client to join a competitive group game
Argue with the client about the behavior
Ignore the behavior

rationale.correct: Mania: low stimulation, consistent limits, simple activities and safety.

perOption.a: Lower stimulation and firm limits help control behavior.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia says, "The voices are telling me I'm bad." What is the best response?

options.text: "I don't hear the voices, but I understand they're real to you. What are they saying?"
"There are no voices."
"What do the voices look like?"
"Ignore them and they'll go away."

rationale.correct: Hallucinations: acknowledge the experience, present reality and assess content and safety.

perOption.a: This presents reality without arguing and assesses for command hallucinations.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia is hearing voices. What is the most important thing for the nurse to find out?

options.text: Whether the voices are telling the client to harm self or others
Whether the voices are male or female
How long the client has heard voices
Whether the client enjoys the voices

rationale.correct: Always assess for command hallucinations.

perOption.a: Command hallucinations are a safety risk.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client says, "I'm a famous surgeon and need to operate today." What is the best response?

options.text: Avoid arguing and focus on the feelings or a reality-based topic
"You're not a surgeon. You're a patient."
"Which operation will you do?"
Laugh along with the client

rationale.correct: Delusions: don't argue or agree; focus on feelings and reality.

perOption.a: Arguing reinforces delusions; reality-based talk is more helpful.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is a positive or negative symptom of schizophrenia.

rationale.correct: Positive symptoms add (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization); negative symptoms take away (flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia).

perOption.r1:c1: Hallucinations add an experience, so they're positive symptoms.
perOption.r1:c2: Negative symptoms are losses of normal function.
perOption.r2:c2: Reduced emotional expression is a negative symptom.
perOption.r3:c2: This isn't a loss of function.
perOption.r5:c1: Disorganized thinking is a positive symptom.
perOption.r5:c2: This isn't a loss of function.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with paranoia refuses hospital meals, saying the food is poisoned. What should the nurse offer?

options.text: Sealed, prepackaged foods
Force-feeding
A taste of the food from the nurse's plate
No food until the client agrees to eat

rationale.correct: Paranoia: build trust, be consistent and use sealed foods.

perOption.a: Sealed packaging reduces suspicion and supports nutrition.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder tells one nurse she is the only one who understands her and that the other nurses are terrible. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep consistent limits and communication across all staff
Assign only that nurse to the client
Agree with the client about the other staff
Ignore the client's comments completely

rationale.correct: Borderline personality disorder: splitting, impulsivity and self-harm; use consistent limits and DBT.

perOption.a: Consistency counters splitting.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with antisocial personality disorder asks a new nurse for extra privileges and flatters her. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Set firm, consistent limits and enforce unit rules
Grant the privileges to build rapport
Share personal information to build trust
Avoid the client

rationale.correct: Antisocial personality: manipulation; use firm limits and consistent consequences.

perOption.a: Clear limits reduce manipulation.
perOption.d: Consistent engagement with limits is better.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with anorexia nervosa has a heart rate of 42/min, a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L and is dizzy when standing. What is the priority?

options.text: Correcting the physiological instability
Exploring the client's body image
Family therapy
Group therapy

rationale.correct: Anorexia: medical stabilization first (cardiac, electrolytes), then nutrition and psychotherapy.

perOption.a: Bradycardia and hypokalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: Which intervention is appropriate for a client with anorexia nervosa in an inpatient program?

options.text: Supervise meals and observe the client for about 1 hour afterward
Let the client eat alone in their room
Let the client weigh themselves whenever they want
Discuss food and calories at length

rationale.correct: Anorexia: supervised meals, blind weights done consistently and focus on feelings.

perOption.a: This prevents hiding food and purging.
perOption.c: Weights are done consistently by staff.
perOption.d: Focus is on feelings rather than food details.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: Which findings suggest bulimia nervosa?

options.text: Swollen salivary glands, worn tooth enamel and calluses on the knuckles
Severe weight loss with BMI 14
Increased muscle mass
High potassium

rationale.correct: Bulimia: binge-purge cycles, often normal weight, parotid swelling, dental erosion, hypokalemia.

perOption.a: These come from repeated self-induced vomiting.
perOption.b: This is more typical of anorexia.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client is pacing, clenching fists and speaking loudly. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Speak calmly in a low voice, give the client space and offer choices
Apply restraints right away
Stand very close and touch the client's arm
Tell the client to calm down or face consequences

rationale.correct: De-escalation: calm voice, safe distance, offer choices, reduce stimulation.

perOption.a: Verbal de-escalation is the first-line response.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client was placed in seclusion for violent behavior in an emergency. Which action is required?

options.text: Monitor the client closely and get a provider evaluation within the time set by regulation (often within 1 hour)
Leave the client alone until the next shift
Use seclusion as a consequence for breaking rules
Write a PRN seclusion order

rationale.correct: Seclusion and restraint: last resort, time-limited orders, continuous monitoring, release as soon as safe.

perOption.a: Seclusion requires ongoing monitoring, a timely face-to-face evaluation and documentation.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: Which feature describes a therapeutic milieu on an inpatient psychiatric unit?

options.text: A structured, safe environment where clients take part in community meetings and activities
Clients stay in their rooms all day
No rules, to promote freedom
Staff make all decisions without client input

rationale.correct: Milieu therapy: structure, safety, community involvement and client responsibility.

perOption.a: The milieu uses the environment and community as part of treatment.
